newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee ends higher for third day.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee ends higher for third day.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures endd higher for the third session in a row Friday, with the nearby May contract seeing a fresh life-of-contract high intraday, though volumes were only moderate.

"CSCE warehouse coffee stocks fell sharply, and you have strikes or potential strikes going on in Brazil and Colombia, so it's hard to imagine how much more bullish you can get," Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said.

"With the May contract heading into first notice day on next Tuesday, 6,678 lots of open interest remaining in the contract, and very little deliverable coffee available, the potential exists for still higher prices," he said.
CSCE May coffee ended up 6.75 cents at 216.55 cents a pound, after seeing a new contract high early at 218.00 cents.
But first notice day for May coffee is April 22 and the July contract now has more open interest.
CSCE July coffee ended up 6.65 cents at 194.15 cents, after seeing a session high at 194.50 cents.
The May/July backwardation ended little changed though at 22.50 cents, not far from Wednesday's contract highs at 22.75 cents seen Wednesday.

Daily momentum oscillators remained very positive, though a standard five day slow stochastic remained overbought around 82 percent, suggesting another downward correction was possible, technical analysts said.
CSCE warehouse stocks fell 16 percent to 67,578 60-kg bags on April 16, down from 80,078 bags, after a 12,500 bag fall in Mexican coffee stocks in the New Orleans warehouses.
Other bullish factors included the threatened Colombian truck drivers strike planned for Sunday and the strikes at the at Brazilian ports, traders said.

The Colombian government has threatened to outlaw the planned truck drivers strike, but traders noted a January strike went ahead despite being declared illegal and disrupted movement of about 200,000 60-kg bags of coffee.
Colombia is expected to ship 600,000-700,000 bags of coffee in April, with about half this amount still to be shipped.

However, a national 48 hour stoppage by Brazilian stevedores, which was to start Friday, had little effect on shipments of agricultural commodities so far, while talks to settle the dispute were scheduled for Friday afternoon.

In other news, Brazilian trade house, Tristao, revised up its estimate of the 1996/97 Brazilian coffee crop to 27.5 million bags from 25.85 million, but estimated next year's 1997/98 crop would slip to 23.5 million bags.

The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) revised down its 1996/97 estimate of Brazil's exportable crop to 15.3 million bags from 16.8 million, and cut its estimate of Brazil's 1997/98 exportable coffee crop to 16.0 million 60-kg bags from an earlier estimate of 17 million.
Coffee prices have surged to their highest levels since 1994 this season, but any relief from higher coffee prices may prove shortlived, analysts said.

Heavy shipments from Latin American origins in the past quarter are likely to abate in the next month as reserves of fresh coffee and stocks are depleted, and the 1996/97 harvests wind down, leaving supplies tight again in the summer.
